subject: working with large datasets in R

messages.author: d8cb910ad0e56cf4
messages.subject: working with large datasets in R
parts:
Hi all!  Im hoping that the collective wisdom can help me get past this hurdle.  Im relatively new to R and am getting a little frustrated as of late. This seems like it should be so simple....

I am using the merge function to do an inner join of two files.   And I get a memory allocation error (for vector size of 822.4mb).  Dimensions of master file is 2 columns x 67447 rows. And the second file has dimension of 3 columns x 3207 rows.  Column 1 is the common column by which I am joining them and then get the error that it could not process due to lack of memory.  I can load each file into R without issue, it is only when I perform the merge function on the data that I get the error.  This is also troubling for when I need to do an analysis on this data....will I get the same error? Ugh.

I am running the 64bit version of R Studio on Windows and have used a computer with both 2GB of RAM and 4GB of RAM with the same problem.  I looked into and tried the ffbase package which is supposed to be more efficient in data handling of large datasets but got the same error (if I did it correct).  And I have been looking into memory profiling as well, but not sure that will solve my problem.  I know people use R to process data much larger than mine and would like to hear some possible solutions from those with more experience.

Any advice or help is appreciated!
Many thanks in advance!
Jill

messages.author: 4b16035cff9b0f8a
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: working with large datasets in R
parts:
(Hi!)

I work with 2GB+ data.frames, so I'm struggling with a lot of the same issues.

4GB isn't enough ram to join a 800MB file, imo. 8GB should do it. 

Once they are joined, you should be able to do analysis, but with only 4GB of ram you are going to perpetually run into memory issues (ask me how I know!). My solution was to work on a cluster machine with much more memory.

You could also build an SQLlite DB and use R to do the join that way.

messages.author: b35e99045f6c74c2
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: working with large datasets in R
parts:
SQLite with RSQLite is your best option — the join with merge() is too much for your memory, but your data are quite small.

RSQLite has helpful convenience functions to make this easy: see the manual, but you can load data into SQLite with dbWriteTable(). Then, it's best if you index the columns you'll be joining on (e.g. your foreign keys). So following the example on page 19 of the RSQLite manual, this would look like:

dbGetQuery(con, "create index row_name_idx on USArrests (row_names)")

Load and index your other table, and then do an inner join, which would look something like:

dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM USArrests, USArrests_2 WHERE USArrests.row_names = USArrests_2.row_names limit 5")

This syntax is usually the easiest for people at first, but you could also use INNER JOIN, or NATURAL JOIN (you probably want a natural join if your merge didn't have by.x= and by.y= specified, this is what merge() does).

HTH,
Vince

messages.author: 8c8f0ca54c4a2459
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: working with large datasets in R
parts:
The data.table package is a very good solution for handling data of this size.  I use it regularly for handling tables with tens to hundreds of thousands of rows.  You have to learn it's slightly different syntax.

The dplyr package is relatively new but is a successor to the plyr package by the same authors. it implements a lot of plyr-style as well as SQL-style operations of data.table style tables (as well as other databases).  I haven't used it but it gets good reviews

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: working with large datasets in R
parts:
I don't think data.table is going to help here, unless she is barely running out of memory at the very end of the join. data.table is faster CPU-wise, but I'm pretty sure they use similar amounts of memory.

One quick thing you can do, since you're running windows, is make sure R is actually taking advantage of all the memory you do have. See here: http://r.789695.n4.nabble.com/How-to-allocate-more-memories-to-R-td2271714.html
